title: Human–artificial intelligence collaboration for comanaging epilepsy in real time
key_facts: Nature Medicine published a University of Pennsylvania paper describing an inpatient prototype that links scalp and intracranial EEG (brain-wave recordings) to a secure large language model that chats with patients through a smartphone app.

The AI processes sleep, medication, cognition and seizure-probability markers, tells patients about clinical events and trends, records symptoms and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector.
It was tested in 13 patients in the epilepsy monitoring unit of the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania (scalp EEG n=11, intracranial n=2).
In a pseudoprospective simulation, fine-tuning with platform annotations cut false alarms by 80.9% and raised the F1 score (a combined accuracy measure) by 158.4%.
Raw seizure alerts were poor: sensitivity 0.136 (8 of 59 clinician-confirmed seizures) and precision 0.138; patient-confirmed annotations had precision 0.71 (5 of 7).
The paper says patients may over-rely on automated systems and that who is responsible for decisions based partly on AI output remains to be settled.
One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures that medication does not control.
quote_evidence: We validated this platform in 13 patients who are undergoing video-EEG monitoring for epilepsy (scalp, n = 11; intracranial, n = 2).
Raw seizure alerts had low sensitivity of 0.136 (8/59) and precision of 0.138 (8/58).
Patients may over-rely on automated systems, and how an interface represents model uncertainty and the AI’s limitations will shape whether patients weigh its outputs appropriately.
why_it_matters_hint: Implanted and wearable epilepsy devices cannot talk to patients in real time today; this tests a chat layer that learns from patients' own feedback, but only in a small hospital study.
notes: Full paper text read (peer reviewed per the journal's own note). Findings come from 13 inpatients at one centre and a simulation; not a trial of a home device.
